metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against Tallying on every single trial. TTB always chooses the option that wins on the most valid discriminating feature, whereas Tallying always chooses the option that wins on a greater number of less valid features. By computing the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the TTB prediction, we can perfectly discriminate between the two models. TTB will yield a high proportion (close to 1, depending on noise), while Tallying will yield a low proportion (close to 0).

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with Take The Best (TTB) on trials where Tallying and TTB make deterministic and opposite predictions. Under TTB, this proportion will be close to 1.0, while under Tallying, it will be close to 0.0, maximizing the discriminability between the two models.

This metric isolates Trial 1, where the two options have exactly 2 positive features each. Tallying sees a perfect 2-vs-2 tie and predicts a 50% probability of choosing either option. However, Weighted Additive (WADD) strongly prefers the first option because its two positive features are the most valid ones (0.95 and 0.85), decisively outweighing the other option's features (0.75 and 0.65). Measuring the proportion of times subjects choose the high-validity option cleanly discriminates the guessing behavior of Tallying from the compensatory, validity-sensitive behavior of WADD.

This metric contrasts choice behavior on Trial 1 and Trial 4. In both trials, Tallying counts an equal number of winning features for Option A and Option B (2 wins each), predicting exactly a 50% chance of choosing A regardless of the beta parameter. Thus, for Tallying, the difference in the probability of choosing A between Trial 1 and Trial 4 is 0. In contrast, WADD weights features by their validities. In Trial 1, Option A wins on the two most valid features (0.95, 0.85), leading WADD to strongly prefer A. In Trial 4, Option A wins on the two least valid features (0.65, 0.55), leading WADD to strongly prefer B. Consequently, WADD predicts a large positive difference between the choice probabilities of A on Trial 1 vs Trial 4, cleanly discriminating the two theories.

Tallying decides based purely on the unweighted count of features. In Trial 1 and Trial 2, Option B has exactly 2 more winning features than Option A, so Tallying predicts the exact same probability of choosing B for both trials. Similarly, in Trial 7 and Trial 8, Option B has exactly 1 more winning feature than A, leading to identical choice probabilities under Tallying. Therefore, the metric (P(B|T1) - P(B|T2)) + (P(B|T7) - P(B|T8)) has an expected value of exactly 0 for Tallying. Conversely, WADD weights features by their subjective validities. Because Option B's features in Trial 1 have higher validities than in Trial 2, and similarly for Trial 7 versus Trial 8, WADD strongly predicts a higher probability of choosing B in the first trial of each pair. This produces a strictly positive expected value for WADD, effectively isolating the difference in how the two models treat feature validities while controlling for raw feature counts.

This metric contrasts the probability of choosing Option A on Trial 1 vs Trial 4. In both trials, Option A and Option B win on an equal number of features (2 vs 2 in Trial 1, 3 vs 3 in Trial 4), so the Tallying heuristic views both as exact ties and predicts a 50% chance of choosing Option A in both cases, leading to a difference of 0. However, in Trial 1, Option A wins on the highest validity cues, whereas in Trial 4, Option B wins on the highest validity cues. WADD is highly sensitive to these validities and will strongly prefer Option A in Trial 1 and Option B in Trial 4, resulting in a large positive difference. This provides a clear, quantitative dissociation between the two theories.

This metric isolates the exact subset of trials where Take-The-Best (TTB) and Tallying make deterministic, but strictly opposite, predictions. It computes the proportion of choices on these trials that are consistent with TTB. Data generated by TTB will yield high values (close to 1.0, bounded only by epsilon lapse rate), whereas data from Tallying will yield low values (close to 0.0, bounded by its own epsilon/temperature noise), creating a maximal and highly reliable contrast between the two models.

This metric isolates 'diagnostic trials' where the Tallying heuristic and the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic make strictly opposite predictions. It measures the proportion of choices on these trials that are consistent with Tallying. For data generated by Tallying, this proportion will be consistently above 0.5 (driven by the core heuristic, diluted only by the lapse rate and softmax temperature). For data generated by TTB, this proportion will be consistently below 0.5 (as the model actively favors the opposite choice, diluted only by its lapse rate). By restricting the metric to these strongly dissociative trials, we maximize the mean difference between theories while keeping between-subject variance low.

This metric calculates the expected value of the product between the subject's choice (+1 for A, -1 for B) and the WADD log-odds score difference for the trial. Because the experimental design deliberately structures 'reversal' trials such that the simple feature count (Tallying) reliably points in the opposite direction of the log-odds weighted sum (WADD), the two theories produce expected scores with opposite signs. For a subject utilizing Tallying, their choices will systematically anti-correlate with the WADD score differences across the experiment, yielding a strictly negative metric value. For a subject utilizing WADD, their choices will positively align with the WADD score differences, yielding a strictly positive metric value. By averaging this continuous measure over all 96 trials, binomial noise is heavily suppressed, ensuring a large mean gap and tight per-subject variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the most valid cue (cue 1) on trials where the options differ on this cue. In this specific experimental design, the first cue is highly predictive (0.98 validity), but whenever it differentiates the options, the remaining cues either exactly tie or collectively oppose it. Under the Compensatory WADD model, the extreme log-odds of the first cue dominate the decision, leading to a high alignment proportion. Under the Tallying model, cues are unweighted; thus, the subject will either guess (when the total number of winning cues is tied) or actively choose the option that loses on cue 1 (when it is outnumbered by the other three cues). Consequently, Tallying predicts an alignment proportion strictly less than or equal to 0.5, while WADD predicts a proportion significantly greater than 0.5.
